title: RAF Delays Force Accident Victims Into Public Hospital Crisis
text: RAF Delays Force Accident Victims Into Public Hospital Crisis Private hospitals are refusing to treat Road Accident Fund claimants due to prolonged invoice settlement times, leaving victims like Ricardo Solomon to endure lengthy waits and sleep in wheelchairs at under-resourced public facilities. Road accident victims are being left in pain as private hospitals and specialists reportedly refuse to treat them under the Road Accident Fund’s undertaking certificates because of delays in settling bills. The undertaking certificate is part of the compensation awarded to successful claimants, allowing them to receive medical treatment from specialists, with the health care providers submitting invoices to the RAF for payment. But repeated delays in settling these invoices have made private health care providers wary of accepting RAF patients. Some pay out of their own pockets and submit claims to the RAF for reimbursement.However, the process can take up to two years. Others, who cannot afford to pay upfront, have to seek treatment at public hospitals. One victim is Ricardo Solomon from Boksburg, Gauteng, who recently spent three nights sleeping in his wheelchair at a public hospital waiting for medical attention for his badly injured leg.“I spent days sleeping in a wheelchair at the public hospital because private doctors and institutions refused to assist me. “I cannot name the hospital because they will target me when I go there again. After the court ruled in my favour almost a year ago, I have been waiting for the payout,” he said. The accident in 2016 left Solomon unable to continue working as a boilermaker.Nearly a decade later, he is still battling complications from his injuries, while financial difficulties have made it difficult to afford medication and support his family. Solomon said doctors had recently diagnosed arthritis in his injured leg, with the pain extending to his hip and back. He said accessing treatment at public hospitals was an exhausting challenge.“When I go to a government hospital, I spend the whole day there. Even if I arrive at 5am, I leave at 6pm,” he said. Solomon is scheduled for a follow-up medical appointment on 25 November, but going from Heidelberg to Boksburg Hospital is an additional financial burden. His medical complications have repeatedly disrupted his attempts to rebuild his working life.Around 2018, after losing his job, Solomon and his family relocated to the Free State, where relatives took them in as they could not support themselves. He later got a job as a bartender and head chef at a hotel.However, his injured leg began swelling severely, forcing him to return to Johannesburg for treatment. The family returned to Johannesburg after he lost his job in the Free State. His mother, a pensioner, helped support them. He subsequently secured employment as a coiler before being promoted to receiving manager within three months.But the physically demands of the job, such as handling heavy copper-wire rolls and moving pallets, put strain on his leg.
